title: One home for each rule
statement: Give each rule one home and authority, restated nowhere else, and check a writer's instructions for contradictions before generating, since conflicting rules cause refusals and silent overrides.
example: A kit instruction to refuse without a source corpus that was never wired took one item type to 0%.
detail: A check-in on why every layer added to an AP question generator had cost quality found the layers fighting each other (`aptraining-local/parallel-ideas-lab/reports/synapse_checkin_2026_05_27_pipeline_quality_paradox.md`, lines 15-19 and 110-123). A kit prompt told the writer to refuse without a source corpus that was never wired, and document questions passed 0% (line 51); a prompt rule demanding four questions clashed with a validator in code enforcing three and was silently overridden, and the writer refused two directives that contradicted each other (lines 91-94); a kit's fixed period framing contradicted the objective's period, and the writer refused (lines 113-114). Earlier the project had put the kit first and the service's own prompt last, as the hard schema authority, so the kit's illustrative field names could not break the judge's JSON shape (`icloud-work/aptraining-crystal-copy-20260521/full-copy/aptraining-root/parallel-ideas-lab/WINS_20260514.md`, line 152). Banned lists count as rules: an intro-video guide keeps its banned punctuation in a settings file and its banned phrases in the script prompt, and restates neither list anywhere else (`downloads/BrainLift - What makes a good intro video.md`, line 953).
against: The banned phrases sit in the generator's prompt, and the AP work found that adding warnings to a generator's prompt made it worse. One case, and the fix was not yet tested when the note was written (same file, line 137).
